findings.title: Removing the multi-provider failure and relying on order() allows non-deterministic/unsafe provider selection
findings.body: Before this change, loading more than one CryptoProvider threw an IllegalStateException, which was a deliberate fail-fast guard against ambiguous crypto configuration. The code now silently keeps the highest-order provider and only debug-logs the others. However DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order() == 200 (see the other files in this PR), so when two of them are on the classpath (for example a FIPS deployment that also pulls in keycloak-crypto-default) the sort leaves their relative order unchanged and the winner is the ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order, which is undefined. The result is that a FIPS deployment can silently select the non-FIPS DefaultCryptoProvider instead of failing, i.e. it silently weakens crypto/compliance guarantee. Equal orders should be detected and rejected (or at minimum given distinct, guaranteed values) rather than resolved by an arbitrary tie-break.

findings.title: Adding order() as an abstract method breaks existing third-party CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: CryptoProvider is a public interface in keycloak-common that external/extension code implements (custom FIPS variants, etc.). Adding `int order();` as a non-default abstract method is a source- and binary-incompatible change: existing implementations will no longer compile, and prebuilt implementations will throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when CryptoIntegration.detectProvider sorts by CryptoProvider::order. Since the interface already uses default methods (getSupportedKeyStoreTypes, getSupportedRsaKeySizes), order() should be declared `default int order() { return 0; }` so existing providers keep working and get a sane default priority.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default KeyStore provider instead of a BouncyCastle provider
findings.body: The method contract (see the interface Javadoc) is to return the BouncyCastle security provider (non-FIPS or FIPS). This implementation returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which is normally SunJSSE/SUN, not BouncyCastle. Any consumer that calls CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getBouncyCastleProvider() and then uses it as a provider argument to Signature.getInstance(..., provider) or similar will get the wrong provider and fail or behave incorrectly. If no BC provider is available, returning null (as WildFlyElytronProvider does) is safer than returning an unrelated provider.

findings.title: Dead/unused encoder calls in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: The two statements `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` create encoders, write into them, and immediately discard the result. They have no effect on the returned value (the actual sequence is built in the following writeDerSeq block) and are leftover code that will confuse maintainers and inflate the method. They should be removed.

findings.title: Test uses a default (P-256) key for all ES256/ES384/ES512, so ES384/ES512 are not exercised realistically
findings.body: The key pair is generated with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, which on standard JDKs defaults to a P-256 key regardless of the algorithm under test. ES384 and ES512 are still run over this P-256 key, so the produced r/s values are only 32 bytes and `integerToBytes(..., len)` just pads them to 48/66 bytes; the real P-384/P-521 cases (where r/s can be 48/66 bytes with leading high bits) are never tested. The round-trip assertion still passes, so the test gives a false sense that the 96- and 132-byte signature paths are validated. Generate a curve-specific key (e.g. `ECGenParameterSpec("secp384r1"/"secp521r1")`) per algorithm.

findings.title: No test covers the new multi-provider ordering/selection logic
findings.body: The core behavioral change of this PR is that detectProvider now sorts providers by order() and picks the highest instead of failing on multiple providers, but there is no test asserting which provider is selected when several are present, nor that the ignored providers are logged. The only added test (ECDSAAlgorithmTest) instantiates AuthzClientCryptoProvider directly and never goes through CryptoIntegration. A test with two registered providers of different order (and ideally an equal-order case) would protect this logic from regressions.
